::: {.lead}
Today you work like in a lab: you do three experiments in Word, Excel and
PowerPoint and record what you see. Do each experiment when your teacher
shows it. After each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy
your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with Word, Excel and PowerPoint, and File
  Explorer.
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the three experiments.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · Three apps and their files

**Aim:** see what each app makes, and the parts that the three apps share.
*(Lesson notes 3.1 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Open `notice-start.docx` in Word. If a yellow bar says *Protected View*,
   click **Enable Editing**. Read the title bar at the top and the status
   bar at the bottom.

   {{< record "Title bar … ; status bar: Page … of …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The title bar shows **notice-start** (some computers also show
   `.docx`). The status bar shows **Page 1 of 1** and the words: **59
   words**. A Word file is a document: pages of text.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="59" unit="words" hint="Look at the left end of the status bar, at the bottom of the window."}
   How many words does the status bar show for the notice?

   Why: The status bar shows Page 1 of 1 and 59 words. A Word file is a document: pages of text.
   :::

2. Open Excel and choose **Blank workbook**. Click the cell **C4**. Read the
   box on the left, above the grid. Then click **+** at the bottom.

   {{< record "The box shows … ; the new worksheet is called …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **C4**: column C, row 4. The new worksheet is **Sheet2**. An Excel file
   is a workbook, and a workbook can have many worksheets.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You click **+** at the bottom of the workbook. What is the new worksheet
   called?

   - [x] Sheet2

     Why: The first worksheet is Sheet1. A workbook can have many worksheets.

   - [ ] Book2

     Why: Book2 is a new workbook (a new file), not a worksheet.

   - [ ] C4

     Why: C4 is the name of a cell: column C, row 4.
   :::

3. Open PowerPoint and choose **Blank Presentation**. Click **New Slide**
   (on the Home tab) two times.

   {{< record "Slides now: … ; the list of slides is on the …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **3 slides**, and the list of slides is on the **left**. A PowerPoint
   file is a presentation: a set of slides.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="3" unit="slides" hint="The blank presentation starts with one slide."}
   You click **New Slide** two times. How many slides are there now?

   Why: 1 + 2 = 3 slides. The list of slides is on the left. A PowerPoint file is a presentation: a set of slides.
   :::

4. In Word, click **File › New**. Type *invitation* in the search box and
   press Enter. Open one template. (No search results? Open any template
   that you see.)

   {{< record "The name of my template" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good answer: the name of the template, for example "Event invitation".
   A template is a ready-made file with a design: you change only the text.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   What is a template?

   - [x] a ready-made file with a design: you change only the text

     Why: You start from the template and add your own content.

   - [ ] an empty document

     Why: A template already has a design and a layout.

   - [ ] a PDF copy of a document

     Why: A PDF is for reading; a template is a start for your own file.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Four commands on the ribbon

**Aim:** find a command by its tab and its group, and write its way.
*(Lesson notes 3.2 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Go back to `notice-start.docx`. Click in the first line (the title).
   Find the command that puts it in the **center** of the line, and click
   it.

   {{< record "The way: Tab › Group › Command" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Home › Paragraph › Center**. The title moves to the middle of the
   line.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which way leads to **Center**?

   - [x] Home › Paragraph › Center

     Why: Center is a common command for a paragraph, so it is on the Home tab.

   - [ ] Insert › Paragraph › Center

     Why: The Insert tab adds things to a file.

   - [ ] Layout › Page Setup › Center

     Why: Page Setup is the setup of the whole page, not of one line.
   :::

2. Click at the end of the last line and press Enter. Add a table with 2
   columns and 3 rows.

   {{< record "The way to Table" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Insert › Tables › Table**: move the mouse over the grid to 2 × 3, then
   click. You *add* a table, so it is on the Insert tab.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Why is **Table** on the Insert tab?

   - [x] You add a table to the file.

     Why: Insert › Tables › Table: the commands that add things are on Insert.

   - [ ] A table is the most common command.

     Why: The common commands for text are on Home.

   - [ ] A table changes the whole page.

     Why: The setup of the whole page is on Layout.
   :::

3. Turn the page sideways (**Landscape**). Then turn it back to
   **Portrait**.

   {{< record "The way to Orientation" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Layout › Page Setup › Orientation**. The setup of the whole page is
   on the Layout tab.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Which tab has each command? Sort them.

   Home
   :   Center

       Why: A common command for text.

   :   Bold

       Why: Home › Font › Bold.

   Insert
   :   Table

       Why: You add a table.

   :   Pictures

       Why: You add a picture.

   Layout
   :   Orientation

       Why: Layout › Page Setup: the setup of the whole page.

   :   Margins

       Why: The margins belong to the whole page too.
   :::

4. Find **Word Count** on the Review tab and click it.

   {{< record "The way … ; the notice has … words" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Review › Proofing › Word Count**: **59 words**, the same number as in
   the status bar. The empty table adds no words.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="Review|the Review tab|Review tab" hint="Its group is Proofing, next to Spelling."}
   On which tab is **Word Count**?

   Why: Review › Proofing › Word Count: 59 words, the same number as in the status bar. The empty table adds no words.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · Save As, PDF and AutoSave

**Aim:** keep your work safe, and make a copy that nobody can change.
*(Lesson notes 3.3 · about 14 minutes)*

1. In the notice, click **File › Save As**. Choose the folder
   **Documents** and the name `2026-11-03_notice_v01` (use today's date).
   Click **Save**. Read the title bar.

   {{< record "The title bar now shows" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The new name, for example **2026-11-03_notice_v01**. Save As made a new
   copy. The start file `notice-start.docx` did not change.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   After **Save As**, what happened to `notice-start.docx`?

   - [x] Nothing: Save As made a new copy with the new name.

     Why: The title bar shows the new name; the start file did not change.

   - [ ] It got the new name.

     Why: The new name belongs to the new copy.

   - [ ] It was deleted.

     Why: Save As never deletes a file.
   :::

2. Click **File › Save As** again. Keep the name, change the type to
   **PDF**, and click **Save**. Open the folder Documents in File Explorer.

   {{< record "The two files: … and …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Two files with the same name and two extensions:
   **2026-11-03_notice_v01.docx** (a Word document) and
   **2026-11-03_notice_v01.pdf** (a PDF). The Word file stays.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which two files are in Documents now?

   - [x] `2026-11-03_notice_v01.docx` and `2026-11-03_notice_v01.pdf`

     Why: The same name, two extensions: a Word document and a PDF. The Word file stays.

   - [ ] only `2026-11-03_notice_v01.pdf`

     Why: Saving a PDF makes a new file; the Word file stays.

   - [ ] `notice-start.docx` and `notice-start.pdf`

     Why: You saved with the new name, in Documents.
   :::

3. Open the PDF (double-click it). Try to change one word of the notice.

   {{< record "Can you change a word? Why?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **No.** A PDF is for reading and printing: the look stays the same on
   every computer. To change the notice, change the `.docx` file and save
   a new PDF.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   You cannot change a word in the PDF. To change the notice, put the steps in
   order.

   1. Open the `.docx` file in Word.
   2. Change the word.
   3. Save the `.docx` file.
   4. Save As PDF again.

   Why: A PDF is for reading and printing: change the Word file, then make a new PDF.
   :::

4. Go back to Word. Look at the **AutoSave** switch at the top left.

   {{< record "AutoSave is … , because …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Usually **Off**: the file is in Documents on this computer, and AutoSave
   works only for files in OneDrive (or SharePoint). So press **Ctrl + S**
   often. (If this computer keeps Documents in OneDrive, the switch is on:
   the same rule.)
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   On a lab computer, AutoSave is **Off**. Why?

   - [x] The file is in Documents on this computer: AutoSave works only for files in OneDrive.

     Why: So press Ctrl + S often.

   - [ ] The file is a PDF.

     Why: The file open in Word is the `.docx`.

   - [ ] Word saves only when you close it.

     Why: Word saves when you press Ctrl + S, or by itself with AutoSave in OneDrive.
   :::
